rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex1.e: Attack: now let us think from Black's side, with Black to move. This position comes from a game played on Lichess. The white queen on a8 is giving check to the black king.
Look at the black queen on b6 and the white king on g1: they stand on the same diagonal, and only the black rook on e3 is between them.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex1.p: Find the move that answers the check and wins material.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex1.c: The rook blocks the check on e8 and leaves the diagonal: now the queen on b6 gives check to the white king.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex1.r: The move is the rook to e8: it blocks the check and opens the diagonal of the queen on b6 to the white king.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex1.e: The queen blocks the check on d8, but it stands in front of the white queen.
With this move White trades queens with check, and the bishop recaptures: Black is still a piece down.
Back to the position: look for the move that blocks the check and, at the same time, opens the diagonal of the queen on b6.
The queen blocks the check on b8, but it stands in front of the white queen.
With this move White captures the queen with check, and Black loses the queen.
Back to the position: look for the move that blocks the check and, at the same time, opens the diagonal of the queen on b6.
The bishop blocks the check on d8, and the rook on e3 stays on the queen's diagonal.
With this move White brings the knight from d3 to c5 and closes the diagonal of the queen on b6. The discovered check is gone, and White is still a piece up.
Back to the position: look for the move that blocks the check and, at the same time, opens the diagonal of the queen on b6.
The king steps out of check to e7, and the rook on e3 stays where it was.
With this move White moves the king off g1, off the diagonal of the queen on b6. The discovered check is gone, and White is still a piece up.
Back to the position: look for the move that blocks the check and, at the same time, opens the diagonal of the queen on b6.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex1.f: That move does not use the queen on b6 on the white king's diagonal. Look for a move of the rook on e3.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex1.v: Try again: the rook on e3 stands between the queen and the white king.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex1.l: White is in check and must answer before anything else. No answer saves the queen on a8, which the rook on e8 attacks.
The knight on d3 blocks the check on c5.
The rook captures the queen on a8. With a single move Black blocked the check, gave check and won the queen.

This is a discovered check: a piece steps off the line between another piece of the same colour and the enemy king, and the check comes from the piece behind. The piece that moves is free to do something else, here block the check and attack the queen.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex2.e: Attack: now with White, in an endgame from a game on Lichess. The black king on h2 is close to the white pieces, and the knight on f2 stands between the rook on d2 and the king. Any knight move gives a discovered check.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex2.p: Find the knight move that leaves the black king defenceless.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex2.c: The knight goes to g4 and gives check to the king. By leaving f2 it also opens the rook's rank: two checks at the same time.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex2.r: The move is the knight to g4: it gives check and, at the same time, opens the check of the rook on d2.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex2.e: The knight leaves f2 and the rook gives a discovered check, but from e4 the knight does not attack the king.
With this move the king goes to h3 and steps out of check. The knight wins nothing more, and the game is level.
Back to the position: look for the knight move that gives check by itself, as well as opening the rook's line.
The knight leaves f2 and the rook gives a discovered check, but from d1 the knight does not attack the king.
With this move the king goes to h3 and steps out of check. The knight wins nothing more, and the game is level.
Back to the position: look for the knight move that gives check by itself, as well as opening the rook's line.
The knight leaves f2 and the rook gives a discovered check, but from d3 the knight does not attack the king.
With this move the king goes to h3 and steps out of check. The knight wins nothing more, and the game is level.
Back to the position: look for the knight move that gives check by itself, as well as opening the rook's line.
The knight gives a discovered check from h3, but it stands next to the black king.
With this move the black king captures the knight, and White is left with just the rook against the rook and four pawns.
Back to the position: look for the knight move that gives check by itself, as well as opening the rook's line.
The knight gives a discovered check on h1, but it stands next to the black king and does not attack the king.
With this move, the black king captures the knight, and White is left with only the rook against the rook and four pawns.
Back to the position: look for the knight move that gives check by itself, besides opening the rook's line.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex2.f: That move does not use the knight standing between the rook and the black king. Look for a knight move.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex2.v: Try again: look for the square from which the knight itself gives check.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.ideia.ex2.l: Against two checks, blocking one of them does not help, and capturing one of the pieces does not either: the other check remains. The king must move, and it only has h3, h1 and g1.
The rook mates on h2, protected by the knight on g4. Had the king gone to h1 or g1, the rook would have mated on d1.
This is a double check: two checks with a single move. Against it the only defence is to move the king, and in positions like this the king has no good square.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.demos.desco: Attack: with White, in a Lichess game. The knight on f5 stands between the queen on c2 and the black king on g6. See what it attacks when it leaves the diagonal.
The knight goes to d6. The queen on c2 gives check to the king, and the knight attacks the black queen on e8.
Black must take care of the king first, and the king goes to g7. The queen on e8 is still attacked.
The knight captures the queen on e8. In a discovered check, the piece that moves can attack another piece, and the opponent only has time to answer the check.
Attack: White again, in another Lichess game. The rook on g1 and the black king on g8 stand on the same file, and only the pawn on g4 is between them. The front piece can also be a pawn.
The pawn captures on f5 and leaves the g-file: the rook gives a discovered check, and the pawn on f5 attacks the queen on e6.
The king goes to h8, and the queen is still attacked.
The pawn captures the queen. The piece that steps aside can be any piece, even a pawn: here, as it moves, it attacks the queen.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.demos.duplo: Attack: White again, in an endgame from a Lichess game. The knight on g5 stands between the rook on g3 and the black king. The black bishop on d5 is attacked by the white king and defended by the pawn on e6.
The knight captures the pawn on e6 and gives check. The rook on g3 gives check too: it is a double check.
The king must move, and it goes to f6. Black has no time to capture the knight or to defend the bishop.
The white king captures the bishop on d5, which lost the defence of the pawn on e6. White won the pawn and the bishop.
Attack: now let us think from Black's side, in another Lichess game. The knight on b2 stands between the rook on a2 and the white king on f2. The white knight on c3 is undefended.
The knight goes to d1 and gives check, and the rook on a2 gives check too: a double check. From d1 the knight also attacks the knight on c3.
The king must move, and it goes to e1.
The knight captures the knight on c3. Black won a piece.
Back to the position: what if the knight went to c4? It also opens the rook's rank, but from c4 it does not attack the king.
The knight goes to c4, and only the rook gives check.

With a single check, White has more defences: the knight on c3 captures the rook on a2, the piece that gave the check. In positions like this, the double check is stronger because it allows neither capturing nor blocking.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.demos.excec: Attack: still with Black, in another Lichess game. The rook on g2 stands between the queen on f3 and the white king on h1, and it can capture the queen on g5 with a discovered check. Does it work here?
The rook captures the queen on g5, and the queen on f3 gives a discovered check.
The rook on f1 captures the queen on f3, the piece that was giving check. Black won one queen and lost the other, and the game is level.

Back to the position: before the discovered check, check whether the opponent can capture the piece giving check, and what that capture costs them. Here the rook on f1 could capture on f3 without losing anything.
Stronger is for the black queen to capture the rook on f1 with check. The rook on f8 defends it.
The rook on e1 recaptures on f1.

The rook on f8 captures on f1 and mates: it covers g1, and the rook on g2, protected by the pawn on h3, closes the other exit. In positions like this, the discovered-check pattern is there, but the strongest move is another one. When the discovered check wins nothing, also remember the discovered attack without check: the front piece moves away, and the one behind attacks a piece.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.pratica.val: The bishop gives a discovered check, but from a8 it attacks nothing, and the white king steps out of check. Look for a move that opens the line of one of your pieces and makes two threats.
The bishop gives a discovered check, but from b7 it attacks nothing, and the white king steps out of check. Look for a move that opens the line of one of your pieces and makes two threats.
The bishop gives a discovered check, but from b3 it attacks nothing, and the white king steps out of check. Look for a move that opens the line of one of your pieces and makes two threats.
The bishop gives a discovered check, but from a2 it attacks nothing, and the white king steps out of check. Look for a move that opens the line of one of your pieces and makes two threats.
The bishop gives a discovered check, but it stands next to the white king, which captures it on c6.
The bishop gives a discovered check, but it stands next to the white king, which captures it on c4.
Your bishop on d5 stands between the rook on h5 and the white king on c5: any bishop move gives a discovered check. Does it work here? Play as Black and find the best move.

The discovered check won nothing: after it the white king steps out of check, and no white piece is left attacked. The pawn on e3 opened the bishop's diagonal to the rook on g2, a discovered attack without check, and threatened to capture on f2. The rook ran to h2, and your rook captured it.
The pawn goes to a4, but it makes no threat, and the game is level. Look for a move that opens the line of one of your pieces.
The pawn captures on f2, but the rook on h2 recaptures it, and the white rook escapes. First capture the rook on h2, which is undefended.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.pratica.des: Now it is your turn. Play as White and find the best move.
The knight left b6 with a discovered check from the queen on g1 and went to d5, from where it attacked the queen on c7. Black blocked the check, and the knight captured the queen.
The knight gives a discovered check, but from c4 it does not attack the queen on c7, and Black blocks the check with the knight on f2. Look for the square from which the knight attacks the queen.
The knight gives a discovered check, but from a4 it does not attack the queen on c7, and Black blocks the check with the knight on f2. Look for the square from which the knight attacks the queen.
The knight gives a discovered check, but from d7 it does not attack the queen on c7, and Black blocks the check with the knight on f2. Look for the square from which the knight attacks the queen.
The knight gives a double check, but from c8 it does not attack the queen. The king goes to b8 and attacks the knight, and Black is better.
The knight gives a discovered check, but the black king captures it on a8.
The queen goes to d4, but the black queen captures the pawn on c2 with check. First use the knight that stands in front of your queen.
The rook captures the bishop, but the black queen captures on c2 with check, and your king is left defenceless.
The queen captures the knight on f2, but the rook on e2 recaptures it. First capture the queen on c7, which your knight attacks.
The pawn captures the bishop, but it opens the c-file: the black queen comes to c2 with check and mates on b2. First use the knight standing in front of your queen.
The pawn captures the bishop, but it opens the c-file: the queen on c7 comes to c2 with check and mates on b2. First capture the queen, which your knight attacks.
The rook captures the bishop, but the queen on c7 captures the pawn on c2 with check and mates on b2. First capture the queen, which your knight attacks.
rot.discoveredAndDoubleCheck.pratica.dup: White again. Play as White and find the best move.
The knight went to d6 and gave a double check, by itself and by the queen on g4. The king had to move, and the knight, which attacked the queen on f7 from d6, captured it.
The knight gives a discovered check, but from d4 it does not attack the queen on f7. Look for the square from which the knight gives check and attacks the queen.
The knight gives a discovered check, but from h4 it does not attack the queen on f7. Look for the square from which the knight gives check and attacks the queen.
The knight gives a discovered check, but from g7 it does not attack the queen on f7. Look for the square from which the knight gives check and attacks the queen.

The knight gives a discovered check and attacks the queen on f7, but on h6 it is pinned by the rook on h8 against your king: it cannot capture the queen. Look for the square from which the knight gives check and attacks the queen.
The knight gives a discovered check, but from e3 it does not attack the queen on f7. Look for the square from which the knight gives check and attacks the queen.
The knight gives a double check, but from e7 it does not attack the queen on f7, and the queen captures it once the king is out of check.
The knight on e4 gives check, but it is a single check, and the pawn on c7 captures the knight. Use the knight that stands in front of your queen.
The rook captures the bishop on f1, but Black is to move: the queen leaves f7 with check on a2, and your double check is gone. First use the knight that stands in front of your queen.
